$comment: Adversarial JCS canonicalisation cases, shared by every implementation.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. Three implementations of RFC 8785 sign or verify the
documents this product puts on the wire, and they are in three different
LANGUAGES, so no single test can import them all:
jcs/jcs.go              Go     — the hub signs with it, the controller
verifies with it, the e2e harness signs
as both with it.
src/lib/offline/jcs.ts  TS     — the app signs offline grant proofs.
proto/vectors/lib.mjs   JS     — generates the conformance vectors.
It used to say the Go side was itself two independent implementations, and
that the independence was the point. It was three copies, and the third
(e2e/jcs.go) missed the json.Number rounding fix and canonicalised 2^53+1
to 2^53 for as long as it existed. Hand-copied implementations are not
independent implementations; they are one implementation and some stale
forks. The Go copies were folded into jcs/. The language boundary is real
and stays, and this file plus proto/vectors/ is how it is held closed.
proto/vectors already cross-checks 93 canonical encodings, but those are
the documents this product actually sends: envelopes of integers and short
strings. Nothing exercised the edges where hand-written canonicalisers
most plausibly disagree — key ordering by UTF-16 code unit, surrogate pairs,
control characters, the ±2^53 boundary, alternative spellings of a number.
The expected values below are derived from RFC 8785 by hand, NOT captured
from any implementation. Captured output would only prove a side
reproduces itself.
A disagreement here is not cosmetic. It means the hub signs bytes the
controller does not re-derive: every command fails at a gate, or a document
differing from the one a human approved verifies anyway.
WHO READS THIS FILE (all of these must stay green):
jcs/cases_test.go                     Go
src/lib/offline/__tests__/jcs.test.ts TS
proto/vectors/verify.mjs              JS
THE `refused` SECTION IS NOT UNIVERSAL — read `js_canonical` there before
assuming it is. Refusal is the Go profile's documented deviation (no
general double formatting); JavaScript gets correct double formatting from
JSON.stringify and accepts what Go refuses. The divergence is pinned per
case rather than left to be rediscovered. See proto/JCS-PROFILE.md.

cases.name: keys sorted by UTF-16 code unit, not by locale
cases.why: 'A' is 0x41 and 'a' is 0x61, so uppercase sorts first. A locale-aware sort puts them together.

cases.name: a non-ASCII key sorts by its code unit, after ASCII
cases.why: é is U+00E9, above every ASCII letter. Sorting by bytes of some other encoding would reorder this.

cases.name: nested objects are sorted at every level
cases.why: An implementation that sorts only the top level passes most real envelopes.

cases.name: array order is preserved
cases.why: Arrays are sequences; sorting them would change the document.

cases.name: an escaped surrogate pair becomes literal UTF-8
cases.why: RFC 8785 emits everything but the short escapes and control characters literally. Mishandling the pair yields two replacement characters.

cases.name: control characters keep their \u00XX form
cases.why: The short escapes are only \b \t \n \f \r \" \\; everything else below 0x20 is \u00XX, lower-case hex.

cases.name: the short escapes are used where they exist
cases.why: Emitting \u0009 instead of \t is valid JSON and the wrong canonical form.

cases.name: an alternative spelling of zero canonicalises to 0
cases.why: Found by fuzzing. 0e00 is a legal JSON number; a canonicaliser that echoed the spelling would sign different bytes for the same value.

cases.name: a positive exponent is expanded
cases.why: 1e2 and 100 are the same number and must produce the same bytes.

cases.name: the largest exactly-representable integer survives
cases.why: 2^53 is the documented upper bound of the deviation note. One past it must be refused, not rounded.

cases.name: a negative integer keeps its sign
an empty key is a key

refused.name: a non-integer number is refused, not rounded
refused.why: The documented Go deviation: full ECMAScript double formatting is not implemented, so a real must be an error rather than a guess. Rounding it would sign a number nobody sent.
refused.js_why: JavaScript is RFC-8785-correct here for free: Number::toString IS the §3.2.2.3 rule. The divergence is one-directional and safe in that direction — anything the app or the generator can produce that Go refuses fails LOUDLY at the Go verifier rather than verifying against different bytes. Nothing in proto/vectors/ contains a non-integer number, and proto/vectors/README.md says not to add one without revisiting this.

refused.name: one past 2^53 is refused
refused.why: Beyond the IEEE-754 safe range the value cannot round-trip, so canonicalising it would silently change it.
refused.js_why: NOT a divergence anybody should be comfortable with, pinned here precisely so it stays visible. JSON.parse rounds 2^53+1 to 2^53 BEFORE the canonicaliser is ever called, so no JS canonicaliser can refuse what it never saw — the value is already gone. Go refuses because it parses with json.Number and applies the bound to the literal. Consequence: never route a JSON document carrying an integer above 2^53 through a JS signer. The app does not (it builds proof objects from typed fields, all unix seconds and short strings) and the generator does not.
